questions.question: An 86-year-old has abrupt fluctuating inattention and confusion after poor intake and a medication change. What is the safest interpretation?
choices: Expected dementia progression
Delirium until a medical evaluation identifies the cause
Normal aging
A psychiatric condition only
questions.explanation: Acute fluctuating change in attention and awareness suggests delirium. Evaluate medical, medication, metabolic, infectious, neurologic, and environmental contributors urgently rather than attributing it to age or chronic dementia.

questions.question: What is the best first approach after an older adult reports a fall?
choices: Assume it was accidental because no fracture is visible
Reconstruct what happened before, during, and after the fall and assess injury, syncope, medications, gait, orthostasis, and environment
Order a sedative for fear of falling
Focus only on age
questions.explanation: Falls are often multifactorial sentinel events. Event reconstruction and a targeted medical, functional, medication, sensory, and environmental assessment guide safer disposition and prevention.

questions.question: Which statement about polypharmacy is most accurate?
choices: Only prescription medications matter
Medication review should include prescriptions, OTC products, supplements, alcohol, nonprescribed substances, actual use, and recent changes
All medications should be stopped immediately after a fall
More medicines always mean better control
questions.explanation: Older adults may have adverse effects or interactions from prescription, OTC, supplement, and substance combinations. Review actual use, indication, dose, prescribers, affordability, and adverse effects before making coordinated changes.

questions.question: A fall that occurs immediately after rising from bed should prompt particular assessment of which factor?
choices: Only bone density
Orthostatic physiology and medication review, along with other fall contributors
A skin biopsy
Food allergy testing
questions.explanation: Position-change falls can relate to orthostatic hypotension, hydration, medication effects, and other contributors. Assess injury and cardiovascular/neuro red flags as well.

questions.question: Why is new functional decline important in geriatric assessment?
choices: It is unavoidable after a certain age
It can be an early sign of acute illness, medication harm, mood disorder, pain, malnutrition, or unsafe conditions
It only matters after hospitalization
It excludes reversible causes
questions.explanation: A change in ADLs/IADLs may be the first observable sign of a medical, medication, cognitive, mood, nutrition, or social problem and should trigger a focused evaluation.

questions.question: Which feature best distinguishes delirium from stable chronic cognitive impairment?
choices: A slow, stable course over years
Acute onset with fluctuating attention and awareness
Need for eyeglasses
A remote family history of dementia
questions.explanation: Delirium typically develops acutely and fluctuates, particularly affecting attention and awareness. Chronic cognitive decline has a different time course, though both can coexist.

questions.question: What is an appropriate response when a frail older adult has unintentional weight loss and weakness?
choices: Assume the cause is aging
Assess nutrition, medical and endocrine disease, mood, pain, sleep, medications, social supports, and functional goals
Prescribe a supplement without assessment
Delay follow-up for a year
questions.explanation: Frailty and weight loss have broad, potentially reversible contributors. Assessment should integrate medical, functional, nutrition, medication, psychosocial, and patient-goal factors.

questions.question: Which finding after a fall most strongly supports emergency evaluation?
choices: A fall without injury and stable function
Head injury with anticoagulant use, loss of consciousness, focal neurologic deficit, persistent vomiting, severe pain, or inability to bear weight
A preference for a different cane
A history of one remote fall
questions.explanation: Head injury, anticoagulant use, syncope, focal neurologic symptoms, persistent vomiting, severe pain, or inability to bear weight may indicate serious injury or medical cause and require urgent/emergency assessment.

questions.question: What is the best interpretation of decision-making capacity in an older adult?
choices: Age alone determines capacity
A dementia diagnosis always eliminates capacity
Capacity is specific to the decision and may fluctuate; evaluate according to the decision and local process
An unwise decision proves incapacity
questions.explanation: Capacity is decision-specific and can fluctuate. Do not equate age, diagnosis, language, or disagreement with incapacity; follow appropriate legal and institutional processes when it is in question.

questions.question: What makes a geriatric outpatient plan safer?
choices: A disease-focused prescription only
Function- and goal-aware follow-up, medication-change monitoring, referral access, caregiver/support assessment, and clear emergency precautions
Avoiding caregiver input
Assuming transportation is available
questions.explanation: Safe geriatric plans account for patient goals, function, supports, medication monitoring, mobility and sensory needs, access barriers, result ownership, and specific reasons to seek urgent care.
